title: 11 Public Speaking Techniques the World's Best Speakers Actually Use
author: Is Public Speaking
summary: The author presents eleven specific, copyable public speaking techniques drawn from the observable practices of world-class speakers across politics, business, entertainment, and performance history. Techniques include creating a performing alter ego, raising your heart rate before speaking, never letting an audience go passive, using strategic silence, preparing the ending of a talk before anything else, and treating every small speaking opportunity as a deliberate practice repetition. The article is explicitly practical and technique-oriented rather than motivational: it argues that the perceived natural talent of great speakers is almost never natural but is the accumulated product of deliberate practice on stages the world never saw. Each technique is grounded in a specific named speaker's actual observed practice. The piece concludes that speaker excellence is a portfolio built through the volume and intentionality of practice, not a gift activated on the day of the big talk.
points: The difference between the speakers you envy and the speakers you have become is not talent — it is a specific set of techniques that the world's best speakers developed, refined, and reused.

Beyonce built 'Sasha Fierce' early in her career to perform with a confidence she did not personally yet feel — research calls this self-distancing, stepping outside yourself to act with more objectivity and less fear.
Taylor Swift trained for the Eras Tour by singing her full setlist on a treadmill every day for months — building muscle memory for delivering a high-energy performance under physical stress.
Most people watch great speakers the way they watch magicians — they see the effect and assume there is no method behind it. There is always a method.
The people who look natural in front of a room are almost never people who waited for the big moment to practice — they are people who treated every small moment as practice for the big one.
quotes: In the 1980 debate with Jimmy Carter, Carter kept referring to voters in the third person: “The American people...” Reagan turned to the camera and said, “Next Tuesday all of you will go to the polls.” Then he asked the line that quietly ended the debate: “Are you better off than you were four years ago?” That word — you — is the entire technique.
The reason is that he is painting an exciting future — self-driving cars, brain chips, Mars — and the fillers make him sound like someone thinking in real time about something huge.
And by the time a real opportunity arrives — the keynote, the pitch, the moment that matters — you have a portfolio behind you that makes the big moment feel like just another rep.
It is a specific set of techniques that the best speakers in history developed, refined, and reused — often deliberately, sometimes by accident, always with intent.
Master your hands Bill Clinton perfected a gesture that came to be called the Clinton thumb — a soft, closed hand with the thumb resting on top, used for emphasis.
Vulnerability is a tool, not a default Sara Blakely opens her Spanx story with the moment she saw panty lines through white pants and decided to solve it herself.
Tony Robbins takes this to an extreme — his audiences clap, yell, repeat phrases, dance, and high-five for hours because he refuses to let the temperature drop.
